topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A server that waits for one client to finish sending a request can become unavailable to everyone else when that client sends only two bytes and stops. Creating a thread for every connection avoids that specific blockage but can exhaust threads and memory under a different workload. Event-driven I/O offers another model: retain connection state and make progress only when an operation is ready.

topics.title: 6.1.1 Interpreting Nonblocking Socket Operations
topics.summary: A nonblocking operation returns instead of waiting indefinitely when it cannot currently make progress. For a socket read, EAGAIN or EWOULDBLOCK means no data is presently available under that operation’s rules. It is not end-of-stream and not a reason to discard a partially decoded message. A zero-length result from a stream receive has a different meaning: the peer has closed its sending direction after available data has been consumed. (R06)

topics.title: 6.1.2 Comparing Reactor and Completion-Oriented Designs
topics.summary: A reactor waits for readiness and then asks the application to perform nonblocking operations. A completion-oriented design submits operations and later receives their completion results. Both need owned buffers, cancellation rules, and limits on outstanding work; the difference is where the pending operation state is represented.

topics.summary: Each connection in the companion owns a descriptor, an incremental decoder, an optional output frame, an output offset, a read/write phase, and an absolute local deadline. blocks.text: The decoder copies received bytes into bounded owned storage. Once a complete request exists, the synchronous handler reads a view valid for the duration of that call. The handler must not retain the view asynchronously. If the architecture later offloads processing, it must transfer an owned request or otherwise extend the input storage’s lifetime.

blocks.text: The connection deadline begins at acceptance and covers frame reception, handler work, and response transmission as checked by the loop. It is not reset every time a client sends one byte. Resetting on each byte can allow a slow sender to retain a connection indefinitely while staying just inside an inactivity timeout.

blocks.text: The deadline is enforced cooperatively by ordinary scheduling. A blocking handler can delay the next deadline check. The SQLite busy timeout bounds one common wait in the teaching application, but the event loop cannot preempt arbitrary callback code. A hard timing guarantee would require a stronger architecture and qualification than this lab provides.

topics.title: 6.2.2 Bounding Admission and Memory
topics.summary: The server admits at most 64 active connections and accepts at most 16 new sockets per loop iteration. Those are explicit teaching limits. A connection that cannot be admitted is closed before allocating a full application operation. This does not make rejection free: the kernel and accept path still consume resources, and a public deployment would require additional front-door controls.

blocks.text: The maximum application frame is 4,096 payload bytes plus a four-byte length header. A connection may also hold an output frame, container overhead, and kernel socket buffers. Multiplying only the payload limit by connection count therefore underestimates total memory. Resource accounting should include both application-owned and kernel-owned costs.

blocks.text: The accept batch limit protects fairness. Without it, a continuous stream of newly arriving connections can keep the loop accepting while existing clients wait for reads or writes. Similarly, a handler that drains one busy socket without a work limit can starve other connections. Fairness policies decide how much progress one participant may make before the loop returns to others.

topics.summary: The server encodes one response and stores its bytes until all have been sent or the connection becomes terminal. Each successful send advances the offset by the returned count. paragraphs: The server encodes one response and stores its bytes until all have been sent or the connection becomes terminal. Each successful send advances the offset by the returned count. MSG_NOSIGNAL is used on Linux to avoid a broken peer turning a write into an unexpected process-wide signal; the send result still has to be checked. (R07)

A successful send establishes that bytes were accepted by the local networking stack, not that the remote application committed an operation. The application protocol’s acknowledgment is a different event. Likewise, a complete response received by the client can arrive after the business operation committed much earlier. These boundaries become crucial when retries are introduced.

On a malformed frame, the decoder marks the connection unusable and the server closes it. Attempting to resynchronize arbitrary malformed bytes can create ambiguous interpretations and additional attack surface. A versioned protocol could define resynchronization deliberately, but this small one-request-per-connection protocol does not.

The deliberate lost-reply failpoint in the worker returns no response after a successful database operation. The transport closes the socket. This is not a random network simulation; it is a controlled way to expose the exact acknowledgment gap the durable retry design must handle.

Keeping these states separate prevents shutdown logic from trying to preserve meaningless partial buffers as durable work.

topics.title: Failure clinic — Resetting the Budget on Every Read
topics.summary: A server grants two seconds to receive a request and resets the timer whenever a byte arrives. A client sends one byte every second. The connection can remain open indefinitely, consuming a slot without completing work. The timer has become an inactivity policy, not a total request budget.

topics.summary: A peer sends only two bytes of the four-byte frame header and remains connected. A blocking server that reads until the whole header arrives can stall every later client. blocks.text: Solution reasoning. A reactor retains separate state for each peer and waits only on readiness, so one incomplete frame does not block every other peer. Admission bounds application state, while a fairness limit prevents a busy listener from monopolizing the loop. A disconnected client changes response delivery, not necessarily the operation’s durable outcome. The correct acceptance condition is continued service plus the documented state of the request, not a blanket assumption of cancellation.
